1.description:
Climate change here describes the wide range of effects resulting from human-caused disruption to atmospheric and oceanic carbon cycling. The influence of humans on the global climate system is primarily due to the emission of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. These effects include rapid global heating, alterations to long-term large-scale climatic patterns such as global circulatory systems, altered local weather patterns, shifts in historic climate regions, and the localised biotic and abiotic responses to these changes.

Note on climate change projections

Modelling is used to project the future impacts of climate change, the exact pathways of which are uncertain due to different possible responses to climate change. Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) are used to project a range of climate change scenarios which account for different concentrations of greenhouse gas emissions resulting from different economic, social and physical responses[123]. This factor page primarily notes the two most extreme scenarios:

  • Best case scenario (RCP2.6): This is the most benign scenario in which future emissions are severely restricted to limit future climate change, although significant change is still projected.
  • Worst case scenario (RCP8.5): This is the most extreme scenario which aligns with the current global emission trajectory.

Under any available scenario average global temperatures will increase with far reaching impacts across the planet during the coming years and decades.

3.impact:
Climate change has compound impacts on other factors. These are briefly laid out below with more detail on each of the relevant factor pages.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Due to climate change having unequal impacts globally, as a result of both physical and socio-economic conditions, international migration of people may increase the UK population and/or change the character of the UK population as a whole. Additionally, there may be increased demand for housing in rural areas as a result of disproportionate population growth and warming in urban areas. As a result, the Peak District may experience changes to the demographic character of both its residents and its visitors due to global and local population changes. There is little research into exactly what these changes may look like, however projections do indicate that current migration trends are likely to be amplified as a result of climate change[64].

Ecological change

The projected impacts of climate change are intrinsically linked to potential ecological changes. As the physical conditions which define species’ niches shift, both spatially and temporally, species distribution and phenology (timing of biological events) will change.

Cooke et al. (2026) model biodiversity change in the UK under a range of climate scenarios up to 2080[61]. They project “extensive community reorganisation” under any scenario with “the disappearance of current bioclimates and emergence of novel ones”. In the Peak District, this is likely to contribute to the local extinction of species, colonisation by novel species, changes to composition of biological communities, increase likelihood of invasive alien species and increased likelihood of pathogens.

Formulating and setting habitat and species targets, as has been the practice for many years, will need to be carefully re-examined as an approach.

Land management practices

Climate change is likely to drive significant and rapid change in land management practices as a result of how land managers and society respond to climate change. Projections from the European Environment Agency indicate that agricultural land value is likely to fall by as much as 80% in southern European and rise by up to 60% northern Europe by 2100, while the UK may see a 20% rise, possibly up to 40% in Scotland[62]. This is indicative of the change in agricultural productivity in these areas; in the UK, land value increase could result in increased arable agriculture to replace lost crop land in southern Europe.

Brown et al. (2022) detail how under different climate change and socioeconomic scenarios, different types of land use change may result, however under all scenarios change is projected[63]. This research indicates that while it is difficult to predict the exact change that may occur, changing land management practise are likely in the Peak District, in part as a response to climate change.

Pollution

The understanding of effect of climate change on pollution is beginning to be better understood, with research in to heavy metal pollution, particulates, sewage release and chemical interactions in their infancy. Uncontrolled vegetation fires, so called ‘wildfire’, is however better understood and a present and growing problem. The increased incidence of wildfires that is likely to result from climate change will cause the emission of more airborne particulate pollution as a result of burnt vegetation. Recent vegetation burning demonstrates that airborne particulate pollution travels large distances and has health impacts beyond the boundary of the Peak District[118] as well as direct impacts on ecosystem services and benefits such as water supply.

Visitation and access

Climate change may directly contribute to increased visitor numbers in the Peak District National Park during heatwave events. As extremes of temperature and humidity are projected to be greater in urban areas[52], people may seek cooler outdoor spaces during these events. Additionally, domestic tourism may increase if the popularity of overseas destinations declines due to extreme heat in countries at lower latitudes, an emerging trend observed in recent warmer years. A study of the impact of heat waves on Spanish tourism showed that during heatwaves, UK tourist number significantly declined, which could indicate that these tourists will increasingly seek domestic tourist destinations like the Peak District during these events[60].

Additionally, it is possible that climate change may result in changes to visitor behaviour, such as a longer peak tourist season and changes to visitor hotspots, as visitors seek out respite from extremes of temperature and humidity. Data, and anecdotal reports from European protected areas and popular tourist destinations around the world, including UK protected areas, are showing extended visitor seasons. Consistent reports indicate a change from traditional seasonal peaks to ‘flatter’ year round visitation patterns, an overall increase in visitor days, and the consequent positive and negative impact on the environment, local communities and local economies.

1.title: Increased average temperature
1.factor_impact_description:
In the Peak District, changes to seasonal temperature patterns are resulting in increased average temperatures throughout the year, with the greatest increases during the summer[49]. Different projections give different forecasts of what the scale of this inevitable change is likely to be going forward, however under all scenarios significant change is still forecast.

Compared to a baseline average temperature for 1981-2010, projections show that:

  • Worst case scenario: By 2035 the Peak District will be experiencing a 1.75oC average temperature increase, which rises to 4.81oC by 2085.
  • Best case scenario: Average temperatures are expected to increase by roughly the same by 2035, and 1.72oC by 2085[50].

Modelling by the National Trust projects that average maximum summer temperatures in the Peak District could increase by up to 5.5oC by 2080 compared to the 1981-2010 baseline, while the average minimum winter temperatures could increase by 2oC for the same period[52].

The most recent State of the UK Climate report published in 2024 showed that this is already taking effect; in the decade 2011-2020 there were 16% fewer days where daily minimum temperature fell below 0 °C compared to the 1981-2010 baseline[53].

2.title: Increased frequency of extreme weather events
2.factor_impact_description:
Extreme events of heat, rainfall, drought and flooding are all projected to continue to increase in the Peak District as a result of global climate change. Compared to the 1981-2010 baseline, projections for the Peak District in 2085 show the number of Met Office-declared heatwave events will roughly double under the best case scenario, or increase 10-fold under the worst case scenario. The number of record wettest months in a year will stay the same in the best case scenario, but will double in the worst case climate scenario. Rivers are much more likely to be in drought under the worst case scenario; the proportion of time rivers are in drought is projected to increase from less than 10% in 1995 to nearly 25% by 2085[50].

Conversely, by 2070 events where hourly rainfall exceeds 30mm per hours (a metric used to forecast flash flood events) are projected to occur twice as often as in 1990[54].

4.title: Changes to seasonal precipitation patterns
4.factor_impact_description:
Seasonal precipitation patterns are also rapidly changing. Best or worst case scenarios indicate that by the 2080s, UK summers could be up to 60% drier while winters could be 30% wetter[54]. Regional modelling also shows that snowfall is also likely to decrease, with fewer days of falling snow[124].

These changes to precipitation are likely to have significant social, ecological and economic impacts including drought, flooding, changes to rivers and groundwater sources, and changed phenology (biological timings), which are further explored below[123].

5.title: Increased summer humidity
5.factor_impact_description:
Global annual maximum daily wet bulb temperature, a measure of humidity, has increased by around 0.2°C each decade between 1973-2022. In summer months in the UK and Europe, daily wet bulb temperature has increased to around 0.3°C each decade over the same period[65].  

In the Peak District, the 1981-2010 baseline indicates that the National Park and its wider region experience low to medium humidity, while projections for 2060-2080 indicate this will increase overall, with disproportionate increases in the lowland and urban areas surrounding the Peak District[52].

6.title: Increased rates of erosion and weathering
6.factor_impact_description:
As a result of the projected changes to temperature and weather patterns outlined above, rates of erosion and weathering to both the natural and built environment are likely to increase. Historic England recognise the causal connection between increased extreme precipitation and dust storms to erosion of heritage assets[55]. In their Independent Assessment of UK Climate Change Risk, the Climate Change Committee outline the risks resulting from increased flooding causing erosion, material degradation and instability. However, they also identify the general lack of detailed projections for erosions and weathering, with more research needed to define links between the climate and weather projects and the actual projected impact of erosion and weathering at the local, regional and national environment level[56].

The National Trust Climate Hazards Map likelihood of landslides data[52] can be used as an indicator of increased rates of erosion due to the multiple causes of landslides that are likely to relate to erosion in the natural and built environments. This data clearly shows that likelihood of landslides in the Peak District increases.

7.title: Increase likelihood of wildfire
7.factor_impact_description:
The Peak District experienced between seven and nine days where the Met Office wildfire danger index recorded “very high” risk conditions during the 1981-2010 period. For the period 2041-2070, this is projected to increase to between 10.5 and 14 days in the best case scenario, and up to 27.5 days per year in the worst case[50]. This indicates that the conditions under which wildfires can ignite and spread are highly likely to become much more common.

In their Wildfire Briefing, UK Climate Risk note that “there are multiple drivers that affect wildfire frequency and intensity including human triggers, vegetation type and wind patterns”[57]. This means that as well as the projected hotter conditions and more frequent periods of drought, compound impacts that increase likelihood of human-caused ignition can also contribute to increased wildfire risk. This could double the risk of wildfire in a 2°C global temperature increase scenario, and quadruple it in a 4°C scenario[57].

3.title: Non-linear climatic change
3.factor_impact_description:
Despite the clear projections outlined above, it is crucial to acknowledge the non-linearity of the Earth’s climatic system. Under all climate scenarios, this can give rise to “unexpected events in the form of abrupt transitions across thresholds, unexpected oscillations, and chaos”[58]. As a result, a much wider range of non-linear, and therefore difficult to project, impacts may result from climate change and cause changes to the Peak District’s key features.

One such important non-linear change may result from changes to the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC). This global circulatory system pays a vital role in keeping the UK warmer than it would otherwise be at its latitude. Melting sea ice and increased rainfall altering oceanic salinity is resulting in the AMOC slowing down, which could result in a series of “tipping point”, or rapid shifts in weather patterns. In the UK, this could ultimately result in cold extremes of -20C[59] should the AMOC shut down entirely.  

While there are indications that the AMOC is already slowing, IPCC research indicates that it is unlikely that it will pass a tipping point threshold before the end of this century. However, other studies indicate there is a chance that it could happen sooner depending on emission scenarios[59]. Complete AMOC shutdown would clearly have huge implications for both human and ecological systems. This emerging science is pointing to the high likelihood of weather pattern impacts in the shorter term from gradual slowing or short-term flow effects.

16.title: Prehistoric monuments and sites
16.key_data: 70% of designated scheduled monuments are prehistoric features. Nine scheduled prehistoric features are considered at risk, while 43 scheduled features are vulnerable. Prehistoric features are found across all Landscape Character Areas of the Peak District indicating their widespread distribution.

21.title: Religious buildings
21.key_data: Historic religious buildings are widespread across the Peak District due to their connection to settlements, and can be found in every Landscape Character Area. There are approximately 100 listed religious buildings in the Peak District. Four religious buildings are considered at risk with an additional three considered vulnerable; over the last five years one religious building has been removed from being at risk indicating an improvement in condition.

24.title: Agricultural landscapes
24.key_data: The majority of the Peak District could be characterised as a heritage farming landscape. Historical farming influences vary greatly across Landscape Character Area due to different patterns of agricultural land management and settlement. There is not a consistent assessment of the heritage farming landscape, however studies show that historical boundary features have historically, and continue to, decline within the National Park.

17.title: Roman and Romano-British sites
17.key_data: 4 of 8 Roman and Romano-British scheduled monuments are considered vulnerable, none are considered at risk. Roman and Romano-British features have been primarily identified in the central, southern and eastern parts of the Peak District.

18.title: Medieval sites
18.key_data: Medieval features are widespread across the Peak District, but designated features are more likely to be in the White Peak. Only two medieval scheduled monument features are considered at risk while nine are vulnerable. This may indicate that this feature-type overall is in relatively good condition, however lack of data about non-designated features makes this difficult to extrapolate.

19.title: 20th century military sites
19.key_data: The distribution of military features in the Peak District may be influenced by proximity to the nearby towns and cities of South Yorkshire, with many training sites clustered on the eastern edge; however, features can be found in a few other parts of the National Park. There are only two designated 20th century military features, neither of which is considered at risk. Due to a paucity of information regarding miliary features it is difficult to draw any overall conclusions about the condition of this feature type.

20.title: Buildings of industry
20.key_data: Buildings of industry are widespread across the National Park, but tend to be clustered around sites of power (e.g. from water) or resource extraction (e.g. mines). There are approximately 13 scheduled monuments and 40 listed buildings of industry in the National Park, with 11 recorded as being at risk. However, lack of up-to-date condition information makes it difficult to draw overall conclusions about the condition of industrial buildings.

22.title: Traditional buildings and settlements
22.key_data: Traditional buildings are widespread across all Landscape Character Areas of the Peak District, present both in traditional settlements as well as more isolated and remote locations. Most traditionally-built and vernacular buildings are not designated. Designated traditional buildings represent the majority of the listed buildings in the Peak District; 39 are considered at risk with a further seven vulnerable. There are no large-scale surveys of traditional and vernacular building in general, although research into farmsteads revealed that compared to national surveys, traditional Peak District farmsteads are in good condition with high levels of survival.

23.title: Country houses and stately homes
23.key_data: Country houses and stately homes can be found across all Landscape Character Areas in the Peak District, but can be seen to be clustered around the Derwent Valley area. Some of the most significant and highly protected buildings in the Peak District are stately homes, including Chatsworth and Lyme Park. There are approximately 40 listed buildings which are stately homes and houses, of which two are at risk and one is vulnerable.

25.title: Quarrying and mining landscapes
25.key_data: Evidence of mining and mineral extraction is widespread across most of the Peak District, however with different characteristics depending on the underlying geology. Little condition data exists for historically quarried and mined sites on the gritstone of the Dark and South West Peak areas, as only one designated scheduled monument quarrying or mining feature is outside of the White Peak or its immediate fringe. Where condition data is available it suggests that some mining landscapes are very vulnerable. The Lead Legacy project showed that around half of undesignated surface lead mining features have been removed entirely.

26.title: Estate lands, parks and gardens
26.key_data: There are 19 recorded historic estates, parks and gardens in the Peak District. Their condition is difficult to assess but may be good, although this raises questions of what condition means for historically designed landscapes, where values around design change over time.  Across the National Park, both within and outside estates, parks and gardens, there are many thousands of significant landscape trees in varied condition, with only a small proportion currently documented.

27.title: Routes through the landscape
27.key_data: There is no comprehensive data available regarding the condition of historic routes in the Peak District, although Reading the Peak District Landscape indicates that routes from the Roman period onwards are widespread across the Peak District. While little evidence regarding the condition of routes as a feature of the heritage landscape is available, listed building and scheduled monument data can give an indication, which suggests overall good condition. However, it is not possible to use this to draw an overall estimate of the condition of historic routes, therefore presenting a large data gap.

28.title: Myths, legends and oral traditions
28.key_data: Due to their intangible nature, it is difficult to link myths, legends and oral traditions to geographic distribution although this can be done through detailed project work. Some are connected to particular places. Examples of projects that support the continuation of this feature include the Derbyshire Folklore website, Bella Hardy's The Dark Peak and the White album, and Studio Skai's project FOLKS: Peak District Folk Tales.

29.title: Local traditions and events
29.key_data: While it is hard to account for, local traditions and events are believed to be widespread across the Peak District. For example, well dressings are taking place in 2026 across 6 of the 8 Landscape Character Areas in the Peak District. It is very difficult to estimate the condition of these traditions and events, but some initiatives aim to record them such as the National Folklore Survey for England which may reveal more detail after research is complete.

30.title: Cultural and social history
30.key_data: Due to its intangible nature, it is very difficult to link cultural and social history to geographic distribution.  Groups and projects in the Peak District seek to record and celebrate this often under recorded aspect of the National Park's cultural heritage, such as Castleton Historical Society and the Hayfield Kinder Trespass Group. However, in other ways this feature could be seen as in decline due to the loss of traditional skills such as locally important building techniques, which is being seen on a national scale.

5.likelihood_text: It is possible that this impact may occur; some damage is already occurring to cultural monuments as a result of these causes and this is expected to continue. However, the most severe results of this impact are less likely within 5-10 years. Cultural monuments are some of the oldest evidence of humans in the Peak District, and therefore have been subject to change for millennia. As a result, a key attribute of them as a feature is that they change over time and it is unlikely that widespread devastating change will take place over the next 10 years.
5.severity: This impact has the potential to be severe due to the compounding effects of its multiple causes, and the fact that it may lead to irreversible changes to the key attributes which contribute to cultural monument features. However, severity has not been rated more highly due to the minor effect some of the causes may have towards this impact. For example, experts suggested that Governance and legislation relating to cultural monuments is not likely to change significantly over the next 10 years.
5.impact: Physical damage to structural remains and earthworks

6.likelihood_text: It is likely that this impact will occur, however as a result of the uncertainty about the location and current condition of buried remains, this is difficult to assess. The causes are likely to occur increasingly over time, especially those related to climate change. This will have compounding impacts overall for soils, and therefore is likely to have knock-on consequences for both known and unknown deposits and remains held in soils.
6.severity: This impact has the potential to be severe, however this is difficult to assess as a result of buried remains by nature being an aspect of this factor which we do not always hold information about, and as a result may not know when they are lost. It is known that the conditions of peat soil preserve buried remains, and that peat soils are significantly at risk from factors such as climate change, and therefore, while it is difficult to draw a direct causal link, this indicates the possibility of this impact being severe.
6.impact: Erosion and degradation of buried remains and soils

7.likelihood_text: This impact may be moderate, due to the potential for changes to some attributes of historic buildings, but the buildings themselves are likely to remain reasonably intact. Historic buildings across the whole Peak District will be impacted, however some areas will be more affected, e.g. in areas of high risk of flooding.
7.severity: This impact is overall possible. However, there is a spectrum over which this impact could occur, with more minor or moderate impacts which do not cause total loss of character of historic buildings being more likely. Additionally, based on current condition data it seems that churches are more likely to be in poor condition, and therefore could be considered more likely to experience impacts.
7.impact: Physical damage to and degradation of buildings

10.likelihood_text: This is the cumulative impact of all of the above impacts, with the potential to be severe as a result of it many compound causes.
10.severity: This impact is possible as a result of it occurring partially but not fully up to 2035.
10.impact: Loss of character and significance of historic buildings

11.likelihood_text: This impact could be severe as it would constitute a significant change to the feature-group and would be widespread and highly noticeable. Landscape integrity is comprised of many different characteristics which are themselves effected more or less by the other impacts described below. Therefore, this impact is in some ways the cumulative result of these other impacts. As a result of the compound effects these impacts could have, loss of integrity of heritage landscapes could be severe.
11.severity: It is unlikely that landscape integrity will be lost up to 2035; there may be changes in landscape integrity associated with the below impacts, and this may result in partial change to landscape integrity in some areas. However, this overall cumulative impact is not expected to occur.
11.impact: Overall loss of integrity of heritage landscapes

12.likelihood_text: This impact could have a moderate effect on the feature-group. Some heritage landscapes are like to be impacted up to 2035; however, this may not be widespread across the whole National Park and may not affect every feature in the feature-group. Additionally, because this impact has a wide range of causes, there may be compound effects resulting in a higher severity of the impact in places where multiple causes take effect, but less severe impact elsewhere.
12.severity: This impact is likely as a result of the contribution of a wide number of causal factors, of which some are projected to occur over the next 10 years.
12.impact: Visual change in character and loss of legibility of heritage landscapes

16.likelihood_text: This impact could be moderate as farming practises are currently in a process of change, which could impact attribute of this feature group, but this is not expected to be significant. Change in wild food plants may impact foraging traditions, however, these are not strong at present anyway.
16.severity: This impact is possible as it may occur, but is more likely with greater significance over a longer timescale than 2035.
16.impact: Change in diet and food-related customs

17.likelihood_text: This be a positive impact on intangible heritage, as continuing to adapt and change makes the continuation of intangible heritage in the Peak District more likely.
17.severity: It is possible that this impact will occur, as intangible heritage is in a constant state of change, however this change is more likely to occur slowly over generations.

2.description: Demographic and sociocultural change refers to features of human populations, for example the distribution of age, race and employment among people in a place. This also includes change to the ways humans interact and relate to each other through behaviour carried out across populations. This may result in changes to the ways people live and care for each other, what people consume, what people think, and what ideologies are dominant or minoritised. These changes can result from or relate to global change such as climate change, changing trends in technology especially relating to communication, and political changes.

4.impact:
Climate change

As outlined on the Climate change factor page, Representative Concentration Pathway modelling accounts for different future greenhouse gas emissions scenarios that result from different responses to climate change. These responses are profoundly shaped by social trends and demographic characteristics. Therefore, all climate change scenarios are intrinsically linked to demographic and sociocultural changes.

Governance and legislation

Potential changes to governance and legislation that impact the National Park are in turn impacted by social trends. For example, the changes in social attitudes to outdoor recreation discussed above could contribute to changes in access legislation if more people demand and campaign for an increased right to countryside access for recreation.

Land management practices

The Shared Socioeconomic Pathways discussion on the Land management practises factor page exemplify how demographic and sociocultural change could impact land management. Under different socio-economic scenarios, these pathways can be used to describe different possible future land use scenarios in the UK.

Visitation and access

Patterns and trends of visitation and access in the National Park are likely to be impacted by changes in the demographic and sociocultural character of both Peak District resident and visitors. This could result in impacts such as change to visitor numbers and changes in the behaviour of visitors due to changing attitudes to outdoor recreation.

8.title: Changes in population size and distribution
8.factor_impact_description: The population within the National Park however has been steadily declining; in 1991 the population was 38,100 and has decreased to 35,837 according to the most recent census estimates (2024)[125]. Future projections of the resident population are heavily dependent on different scenarios, for example resulting from climate change or planning policy. Roughly 16 dwellings a year would be needed to be built and occupied between 2021–2045 to maintain current population levels[126]. Climate change, and the uneven distribution of its impacts, may result in both international and domestic migration which would see higher demand for dwellings in both in the Peak District and in surrounding rural areas due to disproportionate warming and humidity increased in urban areas[52],[64], which could increase the resident population of the National Park.

9.title: Changes to demographic characteristics of residents
9.factor_impact_description:
The demographic characteristics of residents is changing over time in the Peak District National Park, primarily through an aging population resulting from outward migration of younger people and an inward migration of older residents. The local population has a disproportionately high number of residents over the age of 65 compared to national trends and that number is also increasing; 23.6% of the resident population was over the age of 65 in 2011 which has risen to 30% according to the 2021 census data[127].

The declining and aging population is also likely being fuelled by a lack of incentive and infrastructure for younger families to move to the National Park. Average house prices in the Peak District are often higher than local salaries can afford. Based on work commissioned in 2023 for the Peak District Local Plan by Lichfields, the median house price across the Peak District National Park was £342,661 in 2022 compared to much lower figures in the East Midlands (£234,995), the West Midlands (£232,000), and England (£286,000). Across the park between 2013 and 2023 house prices also rose by roughly 63.5%. The ratio of house price to income has also risen across the board, with areas such as the Derbyshire Dales facing a median house price that’s roughly 10 times the median income for the area[126]. This has created an environment where it’s incredibly challenging for new households to move into the Peak District National Park.

Additionally, housing of the size that is appropriate for families are often still owned by older families who are unlikely to move despite under-occupying the property based on its bedroom capacity[126]. Furthermore, commercial agents have identified a lack of community facilities, sports facilities and cultural venues as reasons as to why young people may leave the National Park to begin a career or enter into higher education but not return till they are much older[126].

10.title: Changes in local community service provision
10.factor_impact_description: Changes in service provision are likely to have a compounding effect on demographic and sociocultural change within local communities across the National Park. The previous State of the Park Report (2021) provided the parish of Calver as an example, which over the period of 2010-2020 had lost 4 primary schools, 6 convenience shops and 5 post offices[128]. With a declining and aging population, this can have a knock-on effect on the services provided by local communities as demand decreases and as the working-age population shrinks. This can then have a feedback effect in which areas become less attractive as prospects for younger working-age families, hence compounding the issue of decreasing demand and a reduced workforce population.

11.title: Changes in housing demand and other development pressure
11.factor_impact_description:
Housing demand is likely to have an impact on the demography of the National Park. As discussed above, the pressure for housing development comes from changes to the local population, with overall decline and less young people threatening the sustainability of local communities in the National Park. Current modelling for the Local Plan places housing need at around 16 dwellings per year just to simply keep the population from declining further[126]. A housing figure of 95 new homes a year is modelled to increase the population by 4,247 by 2045; this is identified as providing enough to address population issues and sustain communities. However, a large part of that housing provision would still likely not be affordable housing, so even with more realistic pathways over the next 20 years, there will remain demographic and sociocultural challenges for local communities.

There will also be an additional pressure for greater energy efficiency and carbon reduction in new buildings. The new Future Homes Standard, that is set to come into place in March 2027, will place additional requirements on new dwellings in buildings centrally around carbon efficiency that will be achieved through a combination of low-carbon heating, improved fabric performance, and on-site renewable generation. In practical terms this means that Air Source Heat Pumps will be required in virtually all new dwellings after 2027, as well as some form of renewable energy generation[129].

12.title: Changes in social attitudes to outdoor recreation
12.factor_impact_description:
Social towards the natural environment change overtime. This was evidenced during the Covid-19 Pandemic, which had a profound impact on outdoor recreational participation across the UK. The People and Nature survey conducted by Natural England during the pandemic found that 45% of adults reported spending more time outdoors than prior to the pandemic[130].  Although participation has likely declined from that peak, national surveys suggest that levels of outdoor recreation continue to be higher than pre-pandemic levels and are also closely related to notions of nature connectedness amongst partipants[131],[132].

Additionally, there is anecdotal evidence from Peak District National Park Authority officers and land managers that there has been an increase in less experienced visitors to the National Park, which potentially suggesting outdoor recreation is being taken up by previously underrepresented groups. If occurring, this is a positive change for increasing equality in access to the National Park, however can bring challenges as inexperienced users may not have a full understanding of what is regarded as best practice when visiting green spaces.

3.description:
Ecological change refers to changes within and between species of plants, animals, fungi and microbes resulting from multiple factors including climate change, changing land management practises, and pollution. This could include changes to an individual species behaviour, life cycle, phenology (biological timings), population size, range and intra-species interactions. Consequently, this also includes changes to the species diversity and abundance of ecosystems, altered habitat types and biomes present in a given area, and changes to interactions between species including predation, herbivory, mutualism and parasitism. Where these changes occur, there will be a shift in the functionality of ecological systems resulting in changes to the ecosystem services they deliver.

Note on projection of future climate and socioeconomic scenarios

Research which models future change to ecological communities needs to account for possible future climate change and socioeconomic scenarios, the exact pathways of which are are uncertain due to different possible global, national and local actions. To do this, models for multiple future climate and socioeconomic pathways are used to project a range of possible future scenarios.

Climate models

Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) are used to project a range of climate change scenarios which account for different concentrations of greenhouse gas emissions[123]. This page primarily notes the two most extreme scenarios:

  • Best case scenario (RCP2.6): Future emissions are severely restricted to limit future climate change, although significant change is still projected.
  • Worst case scenario (RCP8.5): Continued current global emission trajectory.

Socioeconomic models

Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) describe a range of scenarios for societal development[100]. This page also references the two extremes of these scenarios as used in ecological research:

  • Sustainability (SSP1): A political and social shift toward environmentally sustainable technological, economic and energy sectors.
  • Fossil-fuelled development (SSP5): Continued production of and demand for fossil fuels for manufacturing.

5.impact:
Climate change

Change in ecological communities could alter the potential for carbon storage in biomass, which will impact the possibility for land-based mitigation of greenhouse gas emissions as is accounted for in net zero targets. For example, changes to blanket bog communities could result in less accumulation of peat soil, reducing carbon storage potential, and in the possible release of additional carbon from soil due to runoff, resulting in enhanced climate change. Ecological communities may also experience non-linear shifts, for example a sudden collapse in function in single biome, which could in turn provoke non-linear climatic impacts due to the impact on water, carbon and nutrient cycling.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Ecological change could impact on the demography and sociocultural practices of both residents and visitors to the Peak District due to the connections between people and their wider ecologies. Shifts in ecological communities could invoke changes to the composition of rural communities, as the possibility for agricultural livelihoods changes and people’s connection to and sense of belonging in the landscape shifts. Additionally, visitors to the Peak District come in part to interact with the ecology of the landscape, from foraging to taking in the view. Changes to these communities may result in different people visiting in different ways.

Land management practices

Land management practices take place in relation to the underlying ecological communities. Therefore, changes to this ecology are likely to result in changed land management practices. For example, in the Peak District, uplands currently managed for grouse moors may be managed differently if the red grouse experiences population decline and the composition upland moorland habitats shift to make this form of moorland management no longer sustainable. Similarly, agricultural practices may have to change if different compositions of agri-ecological systems emerge, pests and diseases impact on crops and livestock, etc.

Pollution

The potential destabilisation of moorland soils as a result of changes to upland vegetation communities could resulting in the wash out of heavy metal pollution stored in these soils from industrial revolution. This would have downstream consequences as this pollution is spread, potentially having further ecological impacts as well as impacting agricultural land and drinking water.

13.title: Reduced population sizes and localised extinction of species
13.factor_impact_description:
Globally, the average size of wildlife populations declined by 73% between 1970 and 2020 while the rate of extinction may be hundreds of times higher than the baseline rate over the last 10 million years[66].

At a local, regional or national scale, reduced population size and localised extinction may result from either an overall extinction of a species, or a shift in its range resulting in extinction from parts of its historic range. Britian already has an extinction debt due to historical factors, meaning that even in the best case climate and socioeconomic scenario, modelling has shown that extinctions of plant species up to 2070 are projected to occur at up to 2.5 times the baseline rate. Under the worst case scenario projections show this could increase to 3.6 times the number of historic extinctions[61].

While these national-scale projections are useful, it is possible that localised extinction rates will be even higher at a regional scale in the Peak District, as shifts in species’ ranges will have a greater impact at a smaller scale.

14.title: Colonisation by novel species
14.factor_impact_description:
The current geographic range of some species’ are likely to shift resulting in colonisation of the Peak District by novel species. This is primarily as a result of climate change and the resultant shifts in localised bioclimates - a description of an area based on “its climatic ability to support predicted species communities”[61]. This may also as a result of accidental or purposeful movement by human. It is challenging to project how this will occur, especially as the ability for species to shift their own range varies greatly. Birds, as a more mobile animal group, have been projected to have an average species range shift of 550km northwards by 2100, with significant reductions in range size and overlap with current habitats[67].

Projections indicate that in Britain, even under the most best case scenario for climate change, 53% of plant bioclimates are likely to be novel by 2070 rising to 89% under the worst case, with worst-case scenario projections for butterflies and birds at 30% and 32% respectively[61]. These projections do not model the mobility of species to adapt their ranges to these shifting bioclimates. However, shifting species range across taxa has already been observed in the UK, with species such as the little egret moving northwards across the UK and the long-winged conehead cricket expanding its range from the south coast into the midlands[67].

Projections for the percentage area of Britain which will be characterised by disappearing and novel bioclimates by 2070 under best-case and worst-case climate scenarios across three taxa: plants, butterflies and birds.

15.title: Changes to composition of biological communities
15.factor_impact_description:
As a result of the projected localised extinction and colonisation by novel species described above, the composition of biological communities is likely to change. Projections indicated that in Britain, across all three taxa which were modelled, species composition will change under either best or worst case climate scenarios, with at least 1.5 times greater change under the more severe scenario[61].

Projections of the percentage change in species composition of plants, butterflies and birds in Britain by 2070.

This change in species composition may result in what have been referred to as “novel ecosystems” which “comprise new species assemblages…[and] have a suite of interactions and processes consistent with a self-organized, functioning ecosystem”[68]. In this ideal scenario, changed composition allows the continuation of ecological functionality.

However, it is also possible that the changed composition of biological communities could cause “ecosystem collapse”, where tipping points in compositional change results in “a critical threshold or tipping point, after which [an ecosystem] can no longer maintain essential functions or structure”[66]. In their Global Assessment Report on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services, the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES) report that, globally, “biological communities are becoming more similar to each other”, which is likely to lead to a loss of ecosystem functionality[69].

16.title: Increase likelihood of invasive species
16.factor_impact_description: As species shift their ranges and take up niches in new locations amongst differently composed communities, it is likely that some species will become invasive and have negative impacts on native, or perhaps novel, ecosystems. The rate of species coming invasive is thought to be increasing globally[69] although there has been little research into changing rates of invasion in the UK. Evidence currently suggests that numbers of invasive species in the UK may increase as a result of the combined effects of climate change, changes to European populations, and human actions[70].

17.title: Increased likelihood of pathogens
17.factor_impact_description: There is likely to be an increase in pathogens affecting native species as well as possible zoonotic disease transmission affecting humans, with climate change contributing to this increased likelihood. Existing trade pathways provide routes for the transmission of pathogens between countries, with climatic changes making it easier for pathogens to become established in the UK[71]. These can have wide reaching ecological consequences, for example tree diseases such as ash dieback contributing to widespread changes to woodlands and the changing composition of biological where one species is disproportionately affected.

18.title: Medieval sites
18.key_data: Medieval features are widespread across the Peak District, but designated features are more likely to be in the White Peak. This may indicate that this feature-type overall is in relatively good condition, however lack of data about non-designated features makes this difficult to extrapolate.

There are only two designated 20th century military features, neither of which is considered at risk. Due to a paucity of information regarding miliary features it is difficult to draw any overall conclusions about the condition of this feature type.

25.key_data: Evidence of mining and mineral extraction is widespread across most of the Peak District, however with different characteristics depending on the underlying geology. Where condition data is available it suggests that some mining landscapes are very vulnerable. The Lead Legacy project showed that around half of undesignated surface lead mining features have been removed entirely.

26.key_data: There are 19 recorded historic estates, parks and gardens in the Peak District. Across the National Park, both within and outside estates, parks and gardens, there are many thousands of significant landscape trees in varied condition, with only a small proportion currently documented.

4.description:
Governance describes systems, processes and mechanisms of taking decisions which inform action taken by organisations, public bodies and other groups, while legislation describes the laws and legal systems to encourage or condemn certain actions. Supporting policy and regulation exist to further clarify, monitor and enforce action. Therefore, governance and legislation result from national, regional, local and organisational decisions regarding which actions are permissible and promoted and which are outlawed.

It is not possible to have much certainty over projections of changes to governance and legislation as this factor is impacted by so many other factors in turn, from popular mood to political power. Therefore, the below projections are sometimes contradictory estimations on possible future changes related to legislation and governance. All carry a relatively low certainty.

6.impact:
Governance and legislation have the potential to impact all other factors due to the legislation and governance frameworks that underlie all action carried out in the UK. This could be drawn together in an almost infinite number of links, however certainty about what impacts are likely is very low, and many relevant ways in which governance and legislation impacts other factors have already been outlined above. Therefore, these are briefly summarised below with some additional impacts that have not yet been noted.

Factor

Possible impacts from governance and legislation

Climate change

Stronger commitments to emissions reduction and carbon sequestration and storage could help to reduce likelihood of global climate change impacts, e.g. changes to the Climate Change Act 2008 or additional global agreements.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Impacts on communities from changes to planning regulation (NFFP, local plan making process etc) could alter housing development in communities, potential knock-on impact to composition of communities.

Ecological change

Possibility for strengthened or weakened environmental protections, e.g. through BNG and biodiversity credits, changes to National Park legislation and governance, etc. Land use framework, LNRSs and 30x30 target may introduce stronger requirements and spatial planning for land to be managed for ecology.

Economy and industry

Changes to farm subsidy schemes may positively or negatively impact he viability of farm businesses. More NSIPs to support low carbon energy and transport infrastructure could support construction and operation jobs.

Land management practices

Farm subsidies and land management grants may incentivise changes to land uses and management actions. Land use framework may change how land use is determined. Changes to land ownership resulting in changed land management may result from enhance community right to buy to England[98].

Possible changes to legislation relating to driven grouse shooting, including further changes to moorland burning regulation about and an ongoing campaign to ban on driven grouse shooting[99], may result to changes in moorland management.

Pollution

Changes to the regulation of sewage waste outflow into freshwater would reduce freshwater pollution. Legislation relating to land management outline above could change agricultural pollution e.g. lower input farming reducing nutrient pollution.

Visitation and access

New access legislation could strength right to access, including permitted activities and areas with open access. Combined authorities may use visitor levies which could impact visitor access by presenting financial barrier, may cause inequality in access.

18.title: Changes to governing legislation and policy of National Parks
18.factor_impact_description:
National Parks in England are enshrined in law through the National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act 1949, with updates to their purposes in the Environment Act 1995. The Landscapes Review, an independent review commission by UK Government and published in 2022, concluded that “purposes and duty for National Parks need reform”[72]. If this were to be carried out, it would result in changes to the foundational legislation of National Parks that guides the action that takes place within them.

The Labour Party’s 2024 Countryside Protection Plan promised to “help National Parks and National Landscapes become wilder and greener, ending the destruction of nature, expanding and restoring habitats”[73], which could indicate that they plan to deliver reform of National Park purposes to support these objectives. Should this happen, it could alter the aims of the Peak District as a National Park, on scale from small and gradual changes to radical shifts in what happens in the National Park. However, whether this happens could be impacted by a change of leadership within the current Labour government or a change in governing party should a General Election by held, as well as priorities of the current government.

19.title: Changes to legal protections and designations of features
19.factor_impact_description:
The individual features and groups of features identified in this report are protected by different legal mechanisms. This currently includes planning policy which enacts the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 to protect historic buildings, environmental protection legislation for example the Environment Act 2021, specific species and habitat protection under the Conservation of Habitats and Species Regulations 2017, protection for public access under the Countryside and Rights of Way Act 2000, and many more pieces of legislation relating to different types of features. Changes to any of these individual pieces of legislation, or the local, regional or national policy and regulation which support them to be enacted could either improve protection for different features, or remove current protection and put these features at greater risk of harm.

It is difficult to project which legislation, policy and regulation may change. Some possible changes based on current political and social trends which relate to different areas of work in to the Peak District are summarised below:

Area

Possible changes in the next 5 years

Built environment planning
  • Pressure for Nationally Significant Infrastructure Project (NSIP) development in the National Park as a result of the Planning and Infrastructure Act 2025[74].
  • Major changes to the National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) resulting in increased development in the National Park[75].
  • Changes to the local plan-making process resulting in altered historic building protections in the Peak District[76].
  • The New Future Homes Standard will come into effect in March 2027, bringing in new requirements around energy efficiency, heating and renewable electricity generation[129].

Environmental protection
  • Changes to requirements for Biodiversity Net Gain meaning changes to recouperation of habitats damaged by development[77].
  • Changes to sewage waste disposal regulation and enforcement following public awareness of pollution from water companies[78].
  • Local Nature Recovery Strategies resulting in more joined up and spatially planned delivery of nature recovery projects[79].

Local communities and the economy
  • NSIP and NPPF changes described above benefitting local communities and economies through house building and support for rural businesses[80].
  • Changes to farm subsidy schemes and other legislation or regulation which effects farm businesses[81].

Access and rights of way
  • Increased public access to the National Park through new access legislation, such as adopting a “Scottish model” of the right to responsible access on all land34.
  • Introduction of visitor levies which charge visitors to the National Park[83].

20.title: New legislation and policy regarding land use in England
20.factor_impact_description:
A Land Use Framework for England was published in 2026 which set out a vision that is likely to shape future legislation and policy regarding land use in England. The actions identified to achieve the vision set out in the framework are likely to shape what kinds of new or updated legislation and policy can be expected as a result of the framework[84].

21.title: Changes to funding for management plan delivery
21.factor_impact_description:
Funding models for delivering the work of National Parks are likely to change. This is considered to be part of the factor of governance and legislation as funding is a key factor in decision making by National Park Authorities (NPAs) and delivery partners.

Current trends are for reduced core (unrestricted) funding allocated by central Government and increased project-specific grant funding and corporate partnerships. Core funding for National Park Authorities for the financial year 2026/27 was cut by 9% compared to previous years[85], following a real term reduction in funding of 40% since 2010[86] which mirrors that experienced by local governments[87]. Project-specific funding, such as the Farming in Protected Landscapes project[88], or corporate partnerships[89] are plugging this funding shortfall.

In the future, this current trend may continue with a decrease in core funding increasing proportion of funding for NPAs and delivery partners coming from project funding and partnerships, as well as the developing markets for off-site Biodiversity Net Gain and carbon and biodiversity credits[90]. Conversely, it is possible that there could be an increase in central government funding for both National Park Authorities and delivery partners. The Landscapes Review called for “the widespread adoption of a new funding model that creates greater long‑term financial stability”[72] while new government schemes could fund work in National Parks by other routes[91].

22.title: Changes to National Park governance
22.factor_impact_description:
The 2022 Landscapes Review makes a recommendation for “reformed governance to inspire and secure ambition in our [protected] landscapes and better reflect society”[72]. This suggested the need for smaller boards, appointed rather than elected chairs, and partnership groups which advise the board, among other recommendations. A Campaign for National Parks report in 2026 further outlines recommendations for reformed National Park governance, with some of the same suggestions as the Landscapes Review[92]. Should these recommendations be taken up, this could result in a considerable shift in power over decision making in National Parks which will influence how features and benefits are protected and managed. However, the likelihood that this will be undertaken is very difficult to determine.

Additionally, devolution and local government reorganisation are already underway, which is likely to continue to change the number and composition of constituent authorities within the Peak District boundary, as well as the transfer of certain powers to new combined authorities[93]. This will therefore impact the governance of these authorities, with consequences for governance within the Peak District. The make-up of the board of the national Park Authority may change, as well as potentially effects for the prioritisation of actions which support the delivery of the National Park’s purposes by statutory authorities. This could be beneficial, especially alongside the enhanced Protected Landscapes duty for relevant authorities[94], which strengthens their responsibility to support the delivery of the purposes. However, it could also result in the deprioritisation of these purposes due to consolidation and reduced staffing. It is not possible to say how likely either of these outcomes are.

21.title: Religious buildings

17.title: Roman and Romano-British sites

18.title: Medieval sites

Only two medieval scheduled monument features are considered at risk while nine are vulnerable. 19.title: 20th century military sites

There are only two designated 20th century military features, neither of which is considered at risk. Due to a paucity of information regarding miliary features it is difficult to draw any overall conclusions about the condition of this feature type.

20.title: Buildings of industry
20.key_data: Buildings of industry are widespread across the National Park, but tend to be clustered around sites of power (e.g. from water) or resource extraction (e.g. mines). There are approximately 13 scheduled monuments and 40 listed buildings of industry in the National Park, with 11 recorded as being at risk. However, lack of up-to-date condition information makes it difficult to draw overall conclusions about the condition of industrial buildings.

22.title: Traditional buildings and settlements
22.key_data: Traditional buildings are widespread across all Landscape Character Areas of the Peak District, present both in traditional settlements as well as more isolated and remote locations. Most traditionally-built and vernacular buildings are not designated. Designated traditional buildings represent the majority of the listed buildings in the Peak District; 39 are considered at risk with a further seven vulnerable. There are no large-scale surveys of traditional and vernacular building in general, although research into farmsteads revealed that compared to national surveys, traditional Peak District farmsteads are in good condition with high levels of survival.

23.title: Country houses and stately homes
23.key_data: Country houses and stately homes can be found across all Landscape Character Areas in the Peak District, but can be seen to be clustered around the Derwent Valley area. Some of the most significant and highly protected buildings in the Peak District are stately homes, including Chatsworth and Lyme Park. There are approximately 40 listed buildings which are stately homes and houses, of which two are at risk and one is vulnerable.

25.title: Quarrying and mining landscapes

Little condition data exists for historically quarried and mined sites on the gritstone of the Dark and South West Peak areas, as only one designated scheduled monument quarrying or mining feature is outside of the White Peak or its immediate fringe. Where condition data is available it suggests that some mining landscapes are very vulnerable. The Lead Legacy project showed that around half of undesignated surface lead mining features have been removed entirely.

26.title: Estate lands, parks and gardens
26.key_data: There are 19 recorded historic estates, parks and gardens in the Peak District. Their condition is difficult to assess but may be good, although this raises questions of what condition means for historically designed landscapes, where values around design change over time.  Across the National Park, both within and outside estates, parks and gardens, there are many thousands of significant landscape trees in varied condition, with only a small proportion currently documented.

27.title: Routes through the landscape
27.key_data: There is no comprehensive data available regarding the condition of historic routes in the Peak District, although Reading the Peak District Landscape indicates that routes from the Roman period onwards are widespread across the Peak District. While little evidence regarding the condition of routes as a feature of the heritage landscape is available, listed building and scheduled monument data can give an indication, which suggests overall good condition. However, it is not possible to use this to draw an overall estimate of the condition of historic routes, therefore presenting a large data gap.

28.title: Myths, legends and oral traditions
28.key_data: Due to their intangible nature, it is difficult to link myths, legends and oral traditions to geographic distribution although this can be done through detailed project work. 5.description: Land management practices are the sets of actions undertaken which shape the ways land is used by people. Different practices will be carried out to achieve different outcomes, such as food production, natural resource extraction or biodiversity conservation. Which outcomes are chosen is affected by who owns, occupies or has the right to manage land, the historical ways the land has been used, both the biological and physical conditions of the area (e.g. underlying geology) as well as economic and socio-cultural factors.

7.impact:
Climate change

As described above, land can be managed to mitigate the impacts of climate change by sequestering or preventing the further emission of fossil fuels. If the Peak District was managed to maximise this, it could help remove CO2 from the atmosphere to slow future climate change. However, on the scale of the Peak District this would have a relatively small impact on global climate change.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Where land management and ownership change, this could have consequences for the demographics of rural and farming communities, based on who is able to live and work in the Peak District. If land is consolidated under fewer ownership, this could mean that fewer people live and work on the land. However, changes to farming or conservation land management practices may result in more rural jobs. Therefore, it is difficult to make projections about exactly what these changes may look like.

Pollution

Certain land management practices can either result in or reduce pollution. Fertiliser run off from agricultural land can cause polluting effects in freshwater systems, and therefore moving toward lower input agricultural land management can reduce this pollution. Land management practices which stabilise soils, for example peatland restoration, can result in reduced top soil runoff and therefore less sediment contaminated with pollutants from industrial air pollution ending up downstream.

Visitation and access

The Peak District is widely known among visitors for its landscapes under their current management regimes, which promote people to visit the area and participate in different recreational activities. If land was managed differently, this could change people’s perception of the landscape and alter their visiting behaviour, as well as possible changes to access infrastructure which would need to adapt around changing land use.  This could be in the direction of reduced access and declining visitation, for example under agriculture intensification, or it could be increased visitation through ecotourism.

23.title: Changes in farming practices
23.factor_impact_description:
The landscape of the Peak District has been shaped by changes in historical farming practices, and future changes are likely to continue this history. Factors such as technology, diversification, subsidy availability, changing climate and trends in diet are likely to result in changes to how food is produced in the Peak District. However, it is difficult to project these changes.

The Government’s Vision for Farming report in 2025 sets out aims to “champion British farming whilst protecting the environment” as well as “supporting our farmers to boost Britain’s food security”[103]. However, under different social, economic and political circumstances there are many changes to farming practices that could result from this vision. The Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (UK-SSPs) developed for the UK Climate Resilience Programme describe some possible futures for farming in the UK.

Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP)

Vision for farming

UK-SSP1: Sustainability
  • Reduced agricultural land area due to reduced meat consumption and sustainable intensification (e.g. urban farming)
  • Improvements in agricultural technology supporting more efficient farming, e.g. GMOs and breeding programmes

UK-SSP5: Fossil-fuelled Development
  • Agricultural consolidation with fewer, larger farms in lowland areas
  • Technology and high-input agriculture supports large increases in yield.

The two extremes on the spectrum of socio-economic pathways for farming in the UK[100].

In the Peak District, at one end of the spectrum it is possible that the future holds a less farmed landscape, with much of the National Park land given over for biodiversity. However at the other extreme, if food security is promoted and climate change makes arable farming in the uplands more feasible, there could an intensive shift towards arable production. Where along this spectrum the future will fall is currently unknown. Using the SSP pathways, projections of land use change by 2080 indicate that in a number of scenarios, the Peak District may become more wooded with a mix of commercial conifer and mixed deciduous woodland, which would be a significant change to present-day farming practices[63] (see below).

24.title: Changes to conservation land management practices
24.factor_impact_description:
Along very similar lines to farming practices, practices which promote land management for ecological conservation are shaped by external factors. Legislation and policy relating to ecological conservation in the UK increasingly promote setting aside land for ecological restoration, for example the 30x30 target and Biodiversity Net Gain policy. Concurrently, there has also been an increased promotion of the coexistence of biological conservation with agriculture in agroecological systems such as agroforestry, as well as conservation grazing systems, for example through farm subsidy schemes such as the Sustainable Farming Incentive. Furthermore, net zero targets for National Parks may indicate a direction of travel towards a greater amount of land managed to reduce land-based carbon emissions (see Governance and Legislation for more detail).

However, as there are many different such approaches, targets and values which shape conservation land management, these may result in a wide variety of practices continuing in the future. In the Peak District, some possibilities are that land may be actively managed towards a more wooded landscape, land could be given over to natural processes with low human input, habitat patchworks and corridors may be promoted, or many other different practices at a variety of scales could take place.

25.title: Changes to ownership & occupation of land
25.factor_impact_description:
Ownership and occupancy of land both effects and is affected by land management practices and may take on a number of changed characteristics in the future dependant on external circumstance. Consolidation of agricultural land under fewer owners is an ongoing trend; in the Peak District there were commercial 224 dairy holdings in 2009 while as of 2025 there are 111 holdings, representing a 51% decrease. However, the number of total cattle being farmed has only decreased by 12%, indicating a large amount of consolidation is occurring[104].

In addition, several factors may cause changes in land value, for example new carbon and biodiversity credit markets, as well as projected increased land value resulting from climate change[62](see below). Changes to land value may promote changes in ownership, which may in turn result in changes to land management practices.

Currently, land in the Peak District is primarily (72%) in private ownership with the remaining 38% owned by the forestry commission, National Trust and other eNGOs, water companies and public bodies, including the Peak District National Park Authority (see below). Changes in the proportion of land held by these major land owners could have significant impacts on the features of the National Park.

26.title: Increased pressure on land use for climate mitigation
26.factor_impact_description: Land management practices can support climate change mitigation in a number of ways, including managing land for carbon sequestration as well as infrastructure for sustainable energy generation, sustainable transport and geoengineering. There may be increasing pressure for land to be managed for the delivery of climate mitigation in these ways. For example, UK Government targets for 95% clean energy generation by 2030 are promoting solar farms, with 157 contracts awarded for new solar farms in February 2026[101]. While these land uses are not exclusive, for example solar farms can also be grazed[102], managing land for energy generation or any other mitigation uses, could have dramatic and wide range consequences for the features of the Peak District.

27.title: Changes to mineral and aggregate extraction
27.factor_impact_description: As with the other possible causes of impact relating to land management described above, it is not possible to project into the future how mineral and aggregate extraction may change in the Peak District or in the UK more widely. Some possible changes could include major new minerals permissions where quarrying or mining and associated infrastructure will impact the Peak District’s features, changes in demand for mineral types or uses, for example if cement production is adapted to be less carbon-intensive, or if current mineral permissions are renewed such as the Hope Valley cement works.

6.description: Pollution is the harmful release or emission, whether accidental or intentional, of substances or energy into the natural environment which can result in harm to organisms, ecosystems or natural functions. This can include air, water, soil, light and noise pollution.

8.impact:
Climate change

Particulate pollution can contribute towards climate change as a result of airborne particulates absorbing heat and light, contributing to atmospheric warming and cloud formation[118].

Ecological changes

Water pollution alters the chemical environment for aquatic life, impacting species’ abilities to reproduce. Excess nutrients or changes to pH cause imbalance with some species thriving at the expense of others, resulting changes to the diversity and composition of aquatic ecosystems. This can also have knock on impacts on terrestrial ecosystems which interact with polluted water sources[119].

Nitrogen air pollution alters lichen community composition, with some species being nitrogen-tolerant and others nitrogen-sensitive. In this was lichens can be used as indicators of nitrogen air pollution[120].

28.title: Air pollution
28.factor_impact_description:
Air pollution can include the emission of particulate matter, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), nitrogen oxides, sulphur dioxides, carbon monoxide, heavy metals and other compounds. Historically these emissions came from industrial pollution however road traffic emissions are now the main source or air pollution[105]. Additionally in the Peak District, both managed and unmanage burning of vegetation can result in the release of particulate matter which can have localised and widespread effects[106].

Trends in vehicle emissions show an ongoing decrease since the 1990s[107], and the increase in electric vehicles may contribute towards further reductions in the future[108]. However, hotter and drier summers as a result of climate change may trap air pollutants and increase the risk of unmanaged burning of vegetation, increasing the emission of particulate pollution in and around the Peak District[108],[109].

29.title: Water pollution
29.factor_impact_description:
Pollutants of water include nitrates and phosphates, primarily from agricultural runoff and sewage outflow[110], as well as both macro- and microplastics[111]. Nitrate pollution rose between 2018 and 2020 and the overall number of water pollution incidents increased by around 17%[112], with an increase in serious pollution incidents 60% in 2024 compared to 2023[113]. Plastic pollution can also be significant in waterways. A survey of 13 UK rivers, including the Trent of which the Peak District’s River Derwent is a tributary, found they all contained plastic pollution, with 28 of 30 sites testing positive for microplastics (less than 5mm)[111]. In National Parks’ specifically, a 2025 report found that there are no unpolluted waterways in any National Park in England[114].

However, ongoing campaigns for stronger regulation on sewage pollution (see Governance and legislation) and possible changes to land management practices which may result in reduce agricultural pollution (see Land management practices) may result in reductions in water pollution in the future.

30.title: Light pollution
30.factor_impact_description: Light pollution can take the form of skyglow, glare or light intrusion resulting from excess artificial light. This can result from road and street lighting, domestic security lighting, businesses, sports grounds and super markets[115]. There is a possibility that increased development both in and around the Peak District may result in increased light pollution. However, measures can be taken so that even where outdoor lighting is necessary, light shielding or timers can reduce overall light pollution.

31.title: Noise pollution
31.factor_impact_description: Noise pollution is primarily caused by transport (road traffic, aircraft and railways) as well as industrial noise[116]. There is little research into soundscape mapping in UK National Parks[117], and therefore it is difficult to assess the current state of noise pollution or how this may change. It is possible that if visitor numbers increase or changes in visitor behaviour occur (see Visitation and access) then noise pollution from visitor travel may increase or change in location and time of year. Additionally, if housing development and Nationally Significant Infrastructure projects occur in the Peak District (see Governance and legislation), there may be noise emissions from construction and ongoing operation of industrial sites.

32.title: Historic industrial pollution
32.factor_impact_description: Historical pollution is a large factor which has impact on the features of the Peak District. This has primarily taken two forms; firstly, air pollution from rapid industrial development in surrounding cities resulting in extensive sulphur deposition on the high Dark Peak moorlands, and secondly, heavy metal pollution from historical mining on the limestone plateau[118]. Soils in these areas retain historic pollutants, and as such in the future, climate change and changes in land management practices which cause soil erosion could cause the release or reactivation of historic pollutants.
