21.title: Religious buildings
21.key_data: Historic religious buildings are widespread across the Peak District due to their connection to settlements, and can be found in every Landscape Character Area. There are approximately 100 listed religious buildings in the Peak District. Four religious buildings are considered at risk with an additional three considered vulnerable; over the last five years one religious building has been removed from being at risk indicating an improvement in condition.

17.title: Roman and Romano-British sites
17.key_data: 4 of 8 Roman and Romano-British scheduled monuments are considered vulnerable, none are considered at risk. Roman and Romano-British features have been primarily identified in the central, southern and eastern parts of the Peak District.

18.title: Medieval sites
18.key_data: Medieval features are widespread across the Peak District, but designated features are more likely to be in the White Peak. Only two medieval scheduled monument features are considered at risk while nine are vulnerable. This may indicate that this feature-type overall is in relatively good condition, however lack of data about non-designated features makes this difficult to extrapolate.

19.title: 20th century military sites
19.key_data: The distribution of military features in the Peak District may be influenced by proximity to the nearby towns and cities of South Yorkshire, with many training sites clustered on the eastern edge; however, features can be found in a few other parts of the National Park. There are only two designated 20th century military features, neither of which is considered at risk. Due to a paucity of information regarding miliary features it is difficult to draw any overall conclusions about the condition of this feature type.

20.title: Buildings of industry
20.key_data: Buildings of industry are widespread across the National Park, but tend to be clustered around sites of power (e.g. from water) or resource extraction (e.g. mines). There are approximately 13 scheduled monuments and 40 listed buildings of industry in the National Park, with 11 recorded as being at risk. However, lack of up-to-date condition information makes it difficult to draw overall conclusions about the condition of industrial buildings.

22.title: Traditional buildings and settlements
22.key_data: Traditional buildings are widespread across all Landscape Character Areas of the Peak District, present both in traditional settlements as well as more isolated and remote locations. Most traditionally-built and vernacular buildings are not designated. Designated traditional buildings represent the majority of the listed buildings in the Peak District; 39 are considered at risk with a further seven vulnerable. There are no large-scale surveys of traditional and vernacular building in general, although research into farmsteads revealed that compared to national surveys, traditional Peak District farmsteads are in good condition with high levels of survival.

23.title: Country houses and stately homes
23.key_data: Country houses and stately homes can be found across all Landscape Character Areas in the Peak District, but can be seen to be clustered around the Derwent Valley area. Some of the most significant and highly protected buildings in the Peak District are stately homes, including Chatsworth and Lyme Park. There are approximately 40 listed buildings which are stately homes and houses, of which two are at risk and one is vulnerable.

7.description: Visitation describes the use of the National Park for leisure and recreation, either by residents or tourists travelling into the Peak District. Access refers to the structures which facilitate this such as paths, tracks, trails, tourism infrastructure and interpretation.

9.impact:
Ecological Change

Visitation and access has the potential to affect ecological change if it leads to impacts such as soil compaction and habitat degradation. Roadside verges have been identified as agricultural settings that may be rich in wildflowers and meadow species can be prone to invasion of more dominant ruderal species due to the nature of disturbance and additional nitrogen that occurs alongside roads and higher levels of traffic[71].

Pollution

If there are changes to visitor numbers, the current prevalence of car travel in how people access the National Park could have an effect on pollution: contributing to carbon emissions as well as noise and light pollution. The knock on demand for car or public transport related infrastructure could also therefore generate further embedded carbon and generate emissions during production.

33.title: Change in number of visitors
33.factor_impact_description:
Due to a variety of trends, it is appropriate to say that the number of visitors to the National Park may be increasing and could increase in the long term. The UK population is currently projected to continue to grow between 2024 and 2034 by roughly 1.7 million[133], amounting to a 2.5% increase. This growth is expected to come exclusively from net migration. The Peak District National Park is uniquely situated between several urban centres that will continue to grow in size. For example, Sheffield is expected to grow by 9.3% by 2032 from 564,000 people to 617,000 and Manchester is expected to grow by 11% in the same period[134]. Given that mobile phone and visitor survey data suggests that 75% of visitors live within a 1-hour drive of the National Park, we can expect that this population growth to likely increase the number of visitors over the next 10 years.

Additionally, based on data provided by Derbyshire County Council from automatic traffic count sites across the National Park, in the period of 2013-2023 traffic flows have remained relatively constant, averaging around 7560 vehicles per day[135]. However, it is important to note that since the 2020 Covid lockdowns, the proportion of workers engaged in hybrid working has steadily increased whilst those who travel to work with no hybrid working arrangements has decreased[133]. This means that despite the traffic flow not dramatically increasing, this data may reveal that an increase in visitors by road has offset the fall in commuter traffic. While this is a plausible explanation, this conclusion is of low certainty as traffic flow count doesn’t account for other evidence.

34.title: Physical impacts resulting from visitors and access
34.factor_impact_description:
Visitors may lead to an increase in likelihood of wildfire. In the most recent visitor survey, 14% of domestic visitors listed having a BBQ as one of the activities they undertook whilst visiting the Peak District National Park[136]. BBQs are recognised as a fire risk[137], however the data certainty is low due to a lack of strong evidence that wildfires are primarily driven by visitor behaviour.

There is a large body of anecdotal evidence that popular destinations across the National Park are facing parking capacity issues leading to verge parking and possible damage to verges and marginal land along roads. Notable incidents have included lorries and emergency services being hindered in the winter of 2025 near Mam Tor as there was an uptick in visitors wishing to view the sunrise/sunset[138].  If visitor numbers and car travel are increasing as is expected, without an increase in access to other modes of transport we can expect this issue to remain prevalent and/or worsen.

There is also evidence to suggest visitors are having a visual impact on the wider landscape. Data collected internally by the Peak District National Park Authority shows frequent reports of fly camping and littering across the National Park[139]. Impacts are typically highly localised and focused around hot spot areas, but there is an obvious immediate visual impact of these incidents that could potentially reduce people’s enjoyment of the special qualities. It’s important to note however, based on 2025 visitor survey results, 98% of visitors continue to believe that the National Park seems well managed and cared for[136].

35.title: Change in patterns of visitor use, engagement and behaviour
35.factor_impact_description:
Whether or not the number of visitors is changing significantly, anecdotally there has been a perception of a change in how visitors engage with the National Park. One of the trends identified has been a greater concentration of visitors at hot spot destinations and reduced visitor seasonality, with visitors coming for more of the year. Data collected internally provides some evidence to this view. Mobile count data in 2024 showed an extended off-peak season from January to March[140], and data collected from the Strava GPS tracking app showed a heavy concentration of users around Mam Tor and the Mam Nik car park[141]. Whether this is representing a largescale shift in how visitors engage with the National Park is hard to say with certainty, as mobile count data only represents certain providers and the Strava data also has inherent self-selection bias as it will only collect data on users who download and actively use the app. Much visitor related data also has a limited time-range of only a few years so it is difficult to establish trends over time.

Changes in how visitors engage and receive information about the National Park may be changing, and could explain higher levels of tourist flow concentration around certain sites and reduced seasonality. The 2025 visitor survey recorded 37% of visitors using social media as a resource to help make the most of their visit, which was a higher proportion than a recommendation from friends and family (34%), online review platforms (30%) and previous knowledge of the area (22%)[136]. This represents a stark change from the visitor survey in 2015, which had previous knowledge of the area dominating as the primary source of information at 65% of visitors, in comparison to social media which was just 2%[142].

Current research does suggest that social media can have an impact on tourist flow concentration in particular. Social media’s impacts are diverse and complex, with the visitor survey data indicating that is may be changing how visitors engage with information about the National Park. Social media is currently dominated by shared user-generated content which can impel people to visit specific destinations as more visitors share their experiences. This may then motivate an increasing number of visitors to travel and take part in that shared experience[143]. Although we cannot establish an empirical link, this would be part of a plausible explanation for the high levels of visitation recorded at particular hot spots, for example Mam Tor, as images of the sunrise were widely shared and posts about the area have trended on social media sites[144].

25.title: Quarrying and mining landscapes
25.key_data: Evidence of mining and mineral extraction is widespread across most of the Peak District, however with different characteristics depending on the underlying geology. Little condition data exists for historically quarried and mined sites on the gritstone of the Dark and South West Peak areas, as only one designated scheduled monument quarrying or mining feature is outside of the White Peak or its immediate fringe. Where condition data is available it suggests that some mining landscapes are very vulnerable. The Lead Legacy project showed that around half of undesignated surface lead mining features have been removed entirely.

26.title: Estate lands, parks and gardens
26.key_data: There are 19 recorded historic estates, parks and gardens in the Peak District. Their condition is difficult to assess but may be good, although this raises questions of what condition means for historically designed landscapes, where values around design change over time.  Across the National Park, both within and outside estates, parks and gardens, there are many thousands of significant landscape trees in varied condition, with only a small proportion currently documented.

27.title: Routes through the landscape
27.key_data: There is no comprehensive data available regarding the condition of historic routes in the Peak District, although Reading the Peak District Landscape indicates that routes from the Roman period onwards are widespread across the Peak District. While little evidence regarding the condition of routes as a feature of the heritage landscape is available, listed building and scheduled monument data can give an indication, which suggests overall good condition. However, it is not possible to use this to draw an overall estimate of the condition of historic routes, therefore presenting a large data gap.

28.title: Myths, legends and oral traditions
28.key_data: Due to their intangible nature, it is difficult to link myths, legends and oral traditions to geographic distribution although this can be done through detailed project work. Some are connected to particular places. Examples of projects that support the continuation of this feature include the Derbyshire Folklore website, Bella Hardy's The Dark Peak and the White album, and Studio Skai's project FOLKS: Peak District Folk Tales.

29.title: Local traditions and events
29.key_data: While it is hard to account for, local traditions and events are believed to be widespread across the Peak District. For example, well dressings are taking place in 2026 across 6 of the 8 Landscape Character Areas in the Peak District. It is very difficult to estimate the condition of these traditions and events, but some initiatives aim to record them such as the National Folklore Survey for England which may reveal more detail after research is complete.

30.title: Cultural and social history
30.key_data: Due to its intangible nature, it is very difficult to link cultural and social history to geographic distribution.  Groups and projects in the Peak District seek to record and celebrate this often under recorded aspect of the National Park's cultural heritage, such as Castleton Historical Society and the Hayfield Kinder Trespass Group. However, in other ways this feature could be seen as in decline due to the loss of traditional skills such as locally important building techniques, which is being seen on a national scale.
